entries.topicDescription: Structuring the presentation layer: MVVM, unidirectional data flow, MVI, state holders and error handling.

tips.title: MVVM: the UI renders state and the ViewModel owns the logic
tips.content:
In MVVM the View (a Composable, Fragment or Activity) only displays state and forwards user actions. The ViewModel holds the screen's state, contains the presentation logic and talks to the data layer. The Model is the data layer: repositories and data sources.

The rule that keeps it working: the ViewModel never references the View. It exposes state, the View observes it and calls functions on the ViewModel in response to clicks. That is what makes the ViewModel testable without a device and safe across configuration changes.

tips.title: Unidirectional data flow: state goes down, events go up
tips.content:
In unidirectional data flow (UDF), state flows in one direction, from the ViewModel down to the UI, and user actions flow the other way, from the UI up to the ViewModel as events. The UI never changes state directly; it asks the ViewModel, which updates the state, and the new state flows back down.

That gives every piece of state a single owner and a single path, which makes bugs easier to trace and screens easier to test: give the composable a state and check what it shows, then send it an event and check what was reported.

tips.title: MVI: intents in, a reducer produces the next state
tips.content:
MVI (Model-View-Intent) is UDF taken further. The screen has a single immutable state. Every user action is an intent (usually a sealed type), and a reducer is a pure function that takes the current state and an intent and returns the new state.

Because all changes go through one function, the state transitions are explicit and easy to unit test, and you can log or replay intents. The cost is more types and boilerplate than plain MVVM, so it pays off on screens with complex state.

tips.title: Prefer one UI state per screen over many separate flows
tips.content:
When a screen exposes many independent StateFlows (title, list, loading, error), the UI can see them in inconsistent combinations, and each new field is one more thing to collect and wire up.

Combine the sources into one UiState in the ViewModel with combine, and expose that as a single StateFlow. The UI renders a consistent snapshot, and a sealed type for the state removes impossible combinations such as loading and failed together. Tiny, unrelated values that change on their own can still stay separate.

tips.title: Use a plain state holder for UI logic that depends on the UI
tips.content:
Not all state belongs in a ViewModel. State that is tied to the UI and doesn't need to survive process changes or hit the data layer, such as whether a drawer is open, a scroll position, or a search box's text and focus, is best held in a plain class remembered by the composable (a state holder), like LazyListState or DrawerState.

Keep business logic and data access in the ViewModel, and UI element logic in a state holder. A state holder can take a lambda or the ViewModel's state as input, and it makes the composable easier to test and preview.

tips.title: Translate errors at each layer boundary
tips.content:
Each layer should speak its own language about failure. The data layer catches library-specific exceptions (HttpException, IOException, SQLiteException) and turns them into domain errors. The domain and presentation code work with those and never see Retrofit or SQLite types. Only the UI decides how an error looks, and it maps a domain error to a string resource.

That keeps libraries replaceable, keeps ViewModels testable with plain fakes, and keeps user-facing wording and localization in the UI layer.

tips.title: The ViewModel reports that navigation should happen; the UI navigates
tips.content:
A ViewModel must not hold a NavController: the NavController belongs to the UI and holding it in a ViewModel that outlives the UI leaks it and ties the ViewModel to the framework. Instead the ViewModel exposes what should happen next, and the composable performs the navigation.

Model it as a piece of state (a destination the UI consumes and clears) or as a one-time event, and keep the ViewModel free of navigation types so it can be tested by asserting on its output.

tips.title: Split a "god" ViewModel before it becomes untestable
tips.content:
A ViewModel that grows to hundreds of lines, mixes unrelated states and depends on many repositories is hard to read, hard to test and slow to change. Typical signs: several unrelated groups of state, functions that never touch each other's fields, and constructor parameters that only some functions use.

Split by responsibility. Move business rules into use cases, move UI-only logic into state holders, and give independent parts of a screen their own ViewModel or a small collaborator class. The ViewModel then coordinates instead of doing everything.
